annotation.title_clean: Odorveillance and the Ethics of Robotic Olfaction
annotation.title_en: Odorveillance and the Ethics of Robotic Olfaction
annotation.authors_or_issuer: Pitt, J.; Wicaksono, A.N.; Lush, V.; Milanovic, K.; Hoover, S.; Stark, E.
annotation.summary_en: Opinion piece in IEEE Technology and Society Magazine on robotic olfaction (electronic noses). It describes medical benefits but warns of 'odorveillance', covert tracking and identification via volatile organic compound signatures, and calls for legally enforceable regulation to protect privacy, consent and human rights.
key_provisions_or_claims: Robotic olfaction can enable early disease diagnosis but should support rather than replace doctors.
Odorveillance allows covert identification and tracking, including of past presence, without consent.
Employers could covertly screen job applicants by their VOC emissions; no current regulations prevent this.
Informed consent is bypassed since odor emission is involuntary and cannot easily be avoided.
Governmental control and legally enforceable regulations are needed to prevent data misuse and oppression.
